snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Economy Finale Hook: Fiscal: Borrowing. Current: Trade. Capital: FDI. MSP: CACP. IMF: SDR. Phillips: Inflation/Unemployment. BEPS: Tax avoidance.

quick_notes.title: Fiscal Recap
quick_notes.detail: Art 112 (Budget). Deficits : Fiscal (total borrowing), Revenue, Primary (Fiscal - Interest). Finance Commission (Art 280).
quick_notes.explanation: A budget is a yearly financial plan for the government, and Article 112 of the Indian Constitution requires the central government to present this budget to Parliament each year. A deficit means the government does not have enough money from taxes and other income to pay for all its expenses, so it borrows money to cover the gap. The main deficit types are the Fiscal Deficit, which is the total amount the government borrows from all sources; the Revenue Deficit, which happens when the government's daily running expenses are more than its daily income from taxes; and the Primary Deficit, which is the Fiscal Deficit minus the interest the government pays on its previous loans, showing how much it borrows just for new spending. The Finance Commission, established under Article 280 of the Constitution, is a special body formed every five years to recommend how tax money collected by the central government is shared with state governments.

quick_notes.title: Taxation Recap
quick_notes.detail: Direct (Progressive), Indirect (Regressive). GST (101st Amend, 279A). Laffer Curve (Rate, whereas Revenue).
quick_notes.explanation: Taxes are money the government collects from people and businesses to fund public services like roads and schools. Direct taxes, like income tax, are paid directly by the person who earns the money, and they are progressive, meaning the more you earn, the higher percentage of tax you pay. Indirect taxes, like the Goods and Services Tax (GST), are added to the price of goods you buy, and they are regressive, meaning they take a larger share of income from a poor person than from a rich person. GST was introduced by the 101st Amendment to the Constitution, and Article 279A sets up the GST Council, a body that decides the tax rates for different products. The Laffer Curve is an economic theory that shows the relationship between the tax rate (the percentage charged) and the tax revenue (the total money collected); it suggests that if tax rates are too high, people may stop working or investing, so revenue actually falls.

quick_notes.title: External Sector Recap
quick_notes.detail: BOP : Current + Capital. CAD : Trade gap. FDI (Long-term), whereas FPI (Hot Money). Tarapore (Convertibility).
quick_notes.explanation: ExternalSector Recap The Balance of Payments (BOP) is a record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world, and it is divided into two main parts: the Current Account and the Capital Account. The Current Account Deficit (CAD) occurs when a country imports more goods and services than it exports, which is often called a trade gap. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is money invested by a foreign company to set up or buy a long-term business in another country, while Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) is short-term money flowing into stocks or bonds, often called hot money because it can leave quickly. The Tarapore Committee was a group that proposed rules for making the Indian rupee fully convertible on the capital account, meaning people could freely exchange rupees for foreign currency for investment purposes.

quick_notes.title: Global Org Recap
quick_notes.detail: IMF (SDR/WEO). World Bank (WDR). WTO (MFN/Geneva). G20 (Global cooperation).
quick_notes.explanation: The International Monetary Fund, or IMF, is a global organization that helps countries manage their money and avoid financial crises. It uses Special Drawing Rights, or SDRs, which are like a special international currency that countries can exchange for real money, and it publishes the World Economic Outlook, or WEO, a report that predicts how the world economy will grow. The World Bank is a different group that gives loans and advice to poor countries for projects like building roads or schools, and it releases the World Development Report, or WDR, each year on a specific topic like poverty or education. The World Trade Organization, or WTO, makes and enforces the rules for trade between countries, using the Most-Favored-Nation, or MFN, principle which means a country must treat all other WTO members equally, and it was created in Geneva, Switzerland. The Group of Twenty, or G20, is a forum of 19 countries plus the European Union that meets to discuss and improve global cooperation on big issues like the economy and climate change.

topic_title: UPSC REVISION: Fiscal Policy, External & Global Economy
lesson_intro: Today we wrap up 'Indian Economy'. You have mastered the budget, the tax system, the global trade dynamics, and the agricultural backbones of our nation. Economy is the most 'Dynamic' subject in UPSC—it changes every year with the Budget and the Survey. Today, we consolidate the 'Static' concepts that help you decode the 'Current' changes. Let's master the final block of economy today.
